p01-score-sides-title.name: p01-score-sides-title
p01-score-sides-title.text: The sign of the score decides which side of the boundary a point is on

p01-score-sides-ctx.name: p01-score-sides-ctx
p01-score-sides-ctx.text: This unit fixes one boundary: $g(\mathbf x)=\mathbf w^T\mathbf x+b$, $\mathbf w=(1,1)^T$, $b=-0.5$. First see how it splits the plane.

p01-score-sides-src.name: p01-score-sides-src
p01-score-sides-src.text: Source: KP01 lecture §1–§2 (score and zero-score set); points A and B follow the lecture's samples; "zero score needs its own rule" is a lecture [supplement].

p01-score-sides-c0.name: p01-score-sides-c0
p01-score-sides-c0.text: Points with $g=0$ form a line; $g>0$ and $g<0$ lie on either side. Which side are A and B on? Compute the scores first.

p01-score-sides-c2.name: p01-score-sides-c2
p01-score-sides-c2.text: Blue side $g>0$: predict $\omega_1$. Red side $g<0$: predict $\omega_2$.

p01-score-sides-c3.name: p01-score-sides-c3
p01-score-sides-c3.text: A$(1,1)$: $g(A)=1\cdot1+1\cdot1-0.5=1.5>0$, on the blue side, predict $\omega_1$.

p01-score-sides-c4.name: p01-score-sides-c4
p01-score-sides-c4.text: B$(0.4,0.05)$: $g(B)=0.4+0.05-0.5=-0.05<0$, on the red side, predict $\omega_2$. It is very close to the line yet still on the negative side.

p01-score-sides-c5.name: p01-score-sides-c5
p01-score-sides-c5.text: The score only decides "which side". At exactly $g=0$ the point is on the boundary and needs a separate rule (assign to a class, or do not classify).

p02-normal-title.name: p02-normal-title
p02-normal-title.text: How does w relate to the boundary? Walking along the boundary, w has no component

p02-normal-ctx.name: p02-normal-ctx
p02-normal-ctx.text: Take two points $\mathbf q_1,\mathbf q_2$ on the boundary (both with score 0) and look at the inner product of their difference with $\mathbf w$.

p02-normal-src.name: p02-normal-src
p02-normal-src.text: Source: KP01 lecture §3 (two-point displacement proof); choosing the two intercept points for $\mathbf q_1,\mathbf q_2$ is a teaching choice so the inner product can be done mentally.

p02-normal-c0.name: p02-normal-c0
p02-normal-c0.text: Any two boundary points have score $0$: $\mathbf w^T\mathbf q_1+b=0$, $\mathbf w^T\mathbf q_2+b=0$. Subtracting, $b$ cancels.

p02-normal-c1.name: p02-normal-c1
p02-normal-c1.text: Teaching choice: the two intercept points have simple coordinates, so the inner product is mental arithmetic. Both satisfy $x_1+x_2=0.5$.

p02-normal-c2.name: p02-normal-c2
p02-normal-c2.text: Displacement along the boundary $\mathbf t=(0.5,-0.5)^T$. Inner product $\mathbf w^T\mathbf t=1(0.5)+1(-0.5)=0$.

p02-normal-c3.name: p02-normal-c3
p02-normal-c3.text: The inner product is $0$, so $\mathbf w\perp\mathbf t$: $\mathbf w$ is perpendicular to the boundary (the normal vector). This holds for any displacement along the boundary.

p02-normal-c4.name: p02-normal-c4
p02-normal-c4.text: From any point walk $s>0$ along $\mathbf w$: $g(\mathbf x+s\mathbf w)=g(\mathbf x)+s\|\mathbf w\|^2$, the score grows, so $\mathbf w$ points to the positive side. Here $\|\mathbf w\|^2=2$.

p03-distance-title.name: p03-distance-title
p03-distance-title.text: A score is not a distance: divide by the length of w to get the perpendicular distance

p03-distance-ctx.name: p03-distance-ctx
p03-distance-ctx.text: Take A as an example. Split A along the direction of $\mathbf w$ into "foot point $\mathbf p$" plus "how far it went".

p03-distance-src.name: p03-distance-src
p03-distance-src.text: Source: KP01 lecture §4–§5; the foot-point formula is a lecture [supplement], verified by substituting back $g(\mathbf p)=0$.

p03-distance-c0.name: p03-distance-c0
p03-distance-c0.text: Let $\mathbf n=\mathbf w/\|\mathbf w\|$ be the unit normal. The point on the boundary closest to A is the foot point $\mathbf p$: $\mathbf x=\mathbf p+r\,\mathbf n$, where $r$ is the signed distance measured along $\mathbf n$.

p03-distance-c1.name: p03-distance-c1
p03-distance-c1.text: Foot point $\mathbf p=(0.25,0.25)$, on the boundary: $g(\mathbf p)=0.25+0.25-0.5=0$.

p03-distance-c2.name: p03-distance-c2
p03-distance-c2.text: Substitute into the score: $g(\mathbf x)=\mathbf w^T(\mathbf p+r\mathbf n)+b=\underbrace{\mathbf w^T\mathbf p+b}_{0}+r\,\|\mathbf w\|$, so $g=r\|\mathbf w\|$.

p03-distance-c3.name: p03-distance-c3
p03-distance-c3.text: $\|\mathbf w\|=\sqrt2\approx1.4142$, $r(A)=\dfrac{1.5}{\sqrt2}\approx1.0607$. The score $1.5$ is not a distance.

p03-distance-c4.name: p03-distance-c4
p03-distance-c4.text: The origin's distance is a special case: $d=\dfrac{|b|}{\|\mathbf w\|}=\dfrac{0.5}{\sqrt2}\approx0.3536$ (gold dashed). For a general point: $z=|g|/\|\mathbf w\|$.

p04-near-boundary-title.name: p04-near-boundary-title
p04-near-boundary-title.text: B is very close to the boundary yet on the negative side: zoom in

p04-near-boundary-ctx.name: p04-near-boundary-ctx
p04-near-boundary-ctx.text: The score of B$(0.4,0.05)$ is $g(B)=-0.05$, very small. Zoom in near it to see the foot point and distance. The zoom box has its own scale.

p04-near-boundary-src.name: p04-near-boundary-src
p04-near-boundary-src.text: Source: KP01 lecture §5 (B's computation and foot point); the zoom box is an illustration added in this task, its scale differs from the left plot; the predicted side is not the true label.

p04-near-boundary-c0.name: p04-near-boundary-c0
p04-near-boundary-c0.text: B almost touches the line. Which class is it predicted to be? How far is it from the line? Guess first, then zoom in.

p04-near-boundary-izt.name: p04-near-boundary-izt
p04-near-boundary-izt.text: Zoom box: about 0.01 per grid unit, its own scale

p04-near-boundary-c2.name: p04-near-boundary-c2
p04-near-boundary-c2.text: $r(B)=\dfrac{-0.05}{\sqrt2}\approx-0.035355$: the minus sign means the negative side; geometric distance $z=|r|\approx0.035355$. Foot point $\mathbf p_B=(0.425,0.075)$.

p04-near-boundary-c3.name: p04-near-boundary-c3
p04-near-boundary-c3.text: A negative score predicts $\omega_2$, even though the distance to the line is only about $0.035$. This is just the model's prediction, not yet compared with the true label.

p05-scaling-title.name: p05-scaling-title
p05-scaling-title.text: Multiply both w and b by 2: the score doubles; what about the distance?

p05-scaling-ctx.name: p05-scaling-ctx
p05-scaling-ctx.text: The horizontal axis is the signed distance $r$, the vertical axis is the score. A stays at $r\approx1.0607$. Compare the original score with the score after multiplying by 2.

p05-scaling-src.name: p05-scaling-src
p05-scaling-src.text: Source: KP01 lecture §6; $g'=2g$ and $\|\mathbf w'\|=2\sqrt2$ follow from the main example; the angle between lines here is not geometric perpendicularity.

p05-scaling-c0.name: p05-scaling-c0
p05-scaling-c0.text: The original score is $g=r\|\mathbf w\|$, slope $\sqrt2$. After multiplying by 2, $g'=2g$, slope $2\sqrt2$. See what happens at A.

p05-scaling-c3.name: p05-scaling-c3
p05-scaling-c3.text: Distance: $z'=\dfrac{3}{2\sqrt2}=1.0607$, same as before. The score and $\|\mathbf w\|$ double together, the ratio is unchanged; the two lines meet at $r=0$, the boundary did not move.

p05-scaling-c4.name: p05-scaling-c4
p05-scaling-c4.text: Myth: "double the score, double the distance". When comparing different $(\mathbf w,b)$, always look at $\|\mathbf w\|$ too.

p06-variants-title.name: p06-variants-title
p06-variants-title.text: Predict: double only w, or multiply all by $−2$?

p06-variants-ctx.name: p06-variants-ctx
p06-variants-ctx.text: Originally $g=x_1+x_2-0.5$. Compare two changes: (a) multiply only $\mathbf w$ by 2 and leave $b$; (b) multiply both $\mathbf w$ and $b$ by $-2$.

p06-variants-src.name: p06-variants-src
p06-variants-src.text: Source: KP01 lecture §6 [supplement] (enlarging only the weights moves the boundary; multiplying by a negative number flips the sides); the two new lines come directly from algebra.

p06-variants-c0.name: p06-variants-c0
p06-variants-c0.text: Predict first: (a) does the boundary move? (b) what happens to A's score and predicted class?

p06-variants-c1.name: p06-variants-c1
p06-variants-c1.text: (a) Only $\mathbf w$ doubled: $2x_1+2x_2-0.5=0$, that is $x_1+x_2=0.25$ (orange dashed). The boundary moves toward the origin; if $b$ is not scaled too it is not the same line.

p06-variants-c2.name: p06-variants-c2
p06-variants-c2.text: (b) Multiply everything by $-2$: $-2x_1-2x_2+1=0$ is still $x_1+x_2=0.5$ (the same line). But $g'(A)=-3<0$, the blue and red sides swap, and A is predicted $\omega_2$.

p06-variants-c3.name: p06-variants-c3
p06-variants-c3.text: Summary: multiply by a positive $c$: prediction, boundary and signed distance are unchanged. Multiply by a negative number: boundary and geometric distance unchanged, the sides and signed distance flip. $c=0$: the score is 0 everywhere, so the distance formula cannot be used. Changing only $\mathbf w$: the boundary moves.

p07-practice-title.name: p07-practice-title
p07-practice-title.text: Practice: 3x₁ − 4x₂ + 10 = 0. How far is the origin from the line? Which side is (1, 2) on?

p07-practice-ctx.name: p07-practice-ctx
p07-practice-ctx.text: Work it out yourself. Hint: first read off $\mathbf w$ and $b$; divide by $\|\mathbf w\|$ for distance; the side depends only on the sign of the score. Press Next when done.

p07-practice-src.name: p07-practice-src
p07-practice-src.text: Source: KP01 lecture practice; answers computed by build_kp01_en.py (‖w‖=5, d=2, g=5, z=1) and recomputed independently by check_numbers.py.

p07-practice-q.name: p07-practice-q
p07-practice-q.text: (a) How far is the origin from this line?  (b) Is the point $(1,2)^T$ on the positive or negative side? How far from the line? (Hint: read off $\mathbf w,b$ first.)

p07-practice-a3.name: p07-practice-a3
p07-practice-a3.text: Check: the foot point $(0.4,2.8)$ gives $1.2-11.2+10=0$, so it is on the line; the distance is non-negative and the sign of the score matches the predicted side.

p08-summary-title.name: p08-summary-title
p08-summary-title.text: Summary: score gives side, w gives direction, divide by length for distance

p08-summary-ctx.name: p08-summary-ctx
p08-summary-ctx.text: Recall along the main example's line; the five conclusions of this KP are on the right.

p08-summary-e0.name: p08-summary-e0
p08-summary-e0.text: $g(\mathbf x)=\mathbf w^T\mathbf x+b$: the sign decides the side; a zero score needs its own rule

p08-summary-e1.name: p08-summary-e1
p08-summary-e1.text: $\mathbf w\perp$ the boundary and points to the side where the score increases

p08-summary-e3.name: p08-summary-e3
p08-summary-e3.text: Multiplying by a positive number changes nothing; a negative number swaps the sides; changing only $\mathbf w$ moves the boundary

p08-summary-e4.name: p08-summary-e4
p08-summary-e4.text: Open question: training data has only samples and labels, so how do we find $\mathbf w,b$? Next KP: the perceptron

p03-foot-title.text: How is the foot point computed? Why is it the point on the boundary closest to $A$?
p03-foot-title.name: p03-foot-title

p03-foot-ctx.text: The last page gave $\mathbf x=\mathbf p+r\mathbf n$ and $g=r\|\mathbf w\|$. Reversing them gives the foot point $\mathbf p$ from $\mathbf x$.
p03-foot-ctx.name: p03-foot-ctx

p03-foot-src.text: Source: addition to KP01 lecture §4 (foot-point formula and Pythagorean proof of the nearest point); the example reuses $A=(1,1)$, $B=(0.4,0.05)$, $\mathbf w=(1,1)$, $b=-0.5$, recomputed independently. Added page: the original deck gave only numeric foot points, so the derivation is restored from the lecture objectives.
p03-foot-src.name: p03-foot-src

p03-foot-c0.text: $\mathbf p=\mathbf x-r\,\mathbf n=\mathbf x-\dfrac{g(\mathbf x)}{\|\mathbf w\|^2}\,\mathbf w$ (since $r=g/\|\mathbf w\|$ and $\mathbf n=\mathbf w/\|\mathbf w\|$). Check: $g(\mathbf p)=g(\mathbf x)-\dfrac{g(\mathbf x)}{\|\mathbf w\|^2}\|\mathbf w\|^2=0$, so the foot point is on the boundary.
p03-foot-c0.name: p03-foot-c0

p03-foot-c2.text: Why is $\mathbf p$ the nearest? Take any point $\mathbf q$ on the boundary. $\mathbf p-\mathbf q$ runs along the boundary, perpendicular to $\mathbf w$, while $\mathbf x-\mathbf p=r\mathbf n$ is parallel to $\mathbf w$. The two segments are perpendicular, so by Pythagoras $\|\mathbf x-\mathbf q\|^2=\|\mathbf x-\mathbf p\|^2+\|\mathbf p-\mathbf q\|^2$.
p03-foot-c2.name: p03-foot-c2

p03-foot-c4.text: The second term satisfies $\|\mathbf p-\mathbf q\|^2\ge0$, so $\|\mathbf x-\mathbf q\|\ge\|\mathbf x-\mathbf p\|$: the foot point is the boundary point nearest to $\mathbf x$, at distance $|r|=|g|/\|\mathbf w\|$. Equality holds only when $\mathbf q=\mathbf p$.
p03-foot-c4.name: p03-foot-c4

p03-foot-cue1.text: See the green line and dots: the foot points of $A$ and $B$.
p03-foot-cue1.name: p03-foot-cue1

p03-foot-cue2.text: See the orange and red lines: any boundary point $\mathbf q$.
p03-foot-cue2.name: p03-foot-cue2

p03-foot-cue3.text: See the purple card: check Pythagoras with $\mathbf q=(0.5,0)$.
p03-foot-cue3.name: p03-foot-cue3

p03-foot-cue4.text: See the gold star: the foot point is nearest.
p03-foot-cue4.name: p03-foot-cue4
